description: We are Team CodeBlack, Bangladesh’s first all-female robotics team. We started our journey on 2021 to solve real-life problems through robotics and IoT and encourage women to pursue technology.  We secured Global Nominee recognition in the NASA Space Apps Challenge in both 2024 and 2025.  Through research, teamwork, and hands-on learning, we turn ideas into practical solutions and proudly represent Bangladesh internationally.
summary:
We, Team Code Black from Rajshahi, Bangladesh, developed The Black Belt, a wrist-worn prototype and web dashboard that help astronauts track their health during long missions. When medical support from Earth is delayed, crew members need a way to recognize changes between routine check-ins and decide what warrants a closer look.

The band uses optical, motion, and contact temperature sensors to estimate pulse, detect movement, and measure wrist skin temperature. Astronauts log their readings in the dashboard, compare them over time, and share their records with the crew medical officer. They also enter blood pressure readings from a cuff and track their sleep duration. We designed the system to estimate calories burned, count steps on Earth, and track exercise in orbit.
We’re integrating historical ISS radiation measurements from NASA’s RadLab to show spacecraft conditions alongside personal health trends. By bringing routine measurements into one record, The Black Belt helps crews identify changes worth rechecking and gives them a history to refer to when following mission medical procedures.
details:
Project details

The Black Belt is a wrist-worn prototype and web dashboard that help astronauts record and review changes in their health during long-duration missions. When support from Earth is delayed, crew members can use their recent readings to decide what to recheck and what to bring to the crew medical officer.

How it works

The wearable design uses an optical sensor to estimate pulse, a motion sensor to capture movement, and a contact sensor to measure wrist skin temperature. The prototype firmware streams sensor readings to a laptop over USB. In the current workflow, crew members enter readings into the dashboard, where they can review trend charts and export a CSV for sharing. The dashboard also accepts manual cuff blood pressure readings, sleep duration, exercise duration, and self-reported stress.

We designed the system to count steps on Earth, track exercise in orbit, and estimate sleep duration and calories burned. In our video, we use simulated readings to show how the band could send data to the dashboard automatically and how the dashboard could flag a change in pulse. We plan to add browser pairing and automated alerts in a future version.

Tools and hardware

We used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the dashboard and Arduino C++ for the ESP32 firmware. The firmware targets the MAX30102 optical pulse sensor, MPU6050 motion sensor, and TMP117 contact temperature sensor. We used Blender to model the band, export the strap as an STL, and animate how the internal components fit together. The project source is available on GitHub. The Black Belt repository

Design choices and intended impact

We designed The Black Belt around a simple question an astronaut might ask after a shift: What’s changed since my last check-in? The dashboard keeps records in the browser so crew members can review trends without relying on a continuous connection to Earth. We chose wrist skin temperature as a personal trend, kept blood pressure tied to a separate cuff, and focused on exercise in orbit, where step counts are less representative of activity.

We’re also integrating historical ISS DosTel1 radiation measurements from NASA RadLab to put spacecraft conditions alongside crew check-ins. Those measurements describe the spacecraft environment. Individual radiation exposure requires personal dosimetry. Together, the wearable and dashboard give crews a way to document changes, repeat a measurement when needed, and share a clearer record when consulting their medical team.
